insights.title: Start smaller. Learn sooner.
insights.intro: How to define a first release around the one thing your users need most.

sections.heading: Start with a problem, not a feature list.
sections.body: Describe the person you are building for, the task they need to complete and what makes it difficult today. A clear problem statement makes it easier to judge every proposed feature.

sections.heading: Choose one complete user journey.
sections.body: A first release should let someone finish a useful task from beginning to end. Account creation alone is not a product. Account creation followed by the essential action and a clear result can be.

sections.heading: Separate essential from useful later.
sections.body: Make three lists: essential to the first journey, helpful but optional, and later experiments. Keep integrations, reporting and administration in view; they are easy to underestimate when planning only the customer interface.

sections.heading: Define how you will learn.
sections.body: Agree on the questions the first release should answer. Can people complete the task? Where do they stop? What support do they need? Combine usage observations with direct feedback rather than relying on a single number.

sections.heading: Plan the next decision.
sections.body: An MVP is not a promise to build every feature later. It is a way to decide what deserves the next investment. Set a review point, collect evidence and adjust your priorities.

insights.title: Clarity before code.
insights.intro: Why a shared prototype can make your next build easier to understand.

sections.heading: Make assumptions visible.
sections.body: Different people can agree on a feature name while imagining very different experiences. A prototype turns that ambiguity into screens, actions and outcomes everyone can discuss.

sections.heading: Follow the everyday task.
sections.body: Start with the journeys people use most often. Show what happens before and after the ideal path: missing information, an interrupted action, an empty account and a recoverable error.

sections.heading: Use the right level of detail.
sections.body: Early wireframes help decide structure. More detailed prototypes help test wording, hierarchy and interactions. Match the fidelity to the decision you need to make, rather than polishing every screen immediately.

sections.heading: Bring engineering into the conversation.
sections.body: Design and development should inform each other. Discuss data, permissions, integrations and performance early enough that they can shape the experience.

sections.heading: Keep the decisions with the design.
sections.body: Record what was agreed, what is still uncertain and why a direction was chosen. That context makes handover more useful than a collection of screens alone.

insights.title: Automate the right things.
insights.intro: A practical starting point for reducing repetitive work in your business.

sections.heading: Look for repetition and friction.
sections.body: List the tasks that repeatedly move the same information between people or tools. Note the time involved, the error rate you observe and the decisions a person still needs to make.

sections.heading: Improve the process first.
sections.body: Automating an unclear process can make confusion move faster. Agree on the trigger, the required information, the expected outcome and the person responsible for exceptions.

sections.heading: Choose simple rules when they are enough.
sections.body: Not every automation needs AI. Predictable routing, reminders and data synchronisation often work well with explicit rules. AI may help with less structured information, but its output needs evaluation.

sections.heading: Keep a human review path.
sections.body: Identify decisions that need approval, define what happens when confidence is low and make it possible to correct an output. Keep access to sensitive information limited to what the task requires.

sections.heading: Measure a small pilot.
sections.body: Start with a contained workflow and compare the results with how the task works today. Review time saved, errors, exceptions and maintenance needs before expanding.
